title: Inside Every Leader Is a Better One
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece asks why leaders, who work hard to master skills in every other domain of life, often coast on "good enough" when it comes to their own leadership development. The answer offered is complacency born of adequate everyday results — if the leader's approach seems to work well enough by ordinary standards, there's little visible pressure to improve. The article uses a story about legendary wrestling coach Dan Gable, who reportedly answered every aspiring Olympian's request for advice with a single question — "How important is it to you?" — to argue that meaningful improvement in leadership, like in athletics, only happens once a leader genuinely decides it matters enough to sacrifice for.
points: Complacency in leadership development is attributed to leaders judging themselves against an "everyday standard" that feels adequate, not against their real potential.
The Dan Gable anecdote — responding to every aspiring Olympian with "How important is it to you?" — is used to argue that improvement requires a genuine prior decision to prioritize it.
The piece contrasts leaders' willingness to work hard at other skills with their tendency to "celebrate average" specifically in leadership.
The closing line reframes the audience for a leader's improvement — noting that the people being led are the ones "waiting for your answer" about whether change matters.
quotes: Many leaders suggest they want to be better but fail to put in the time or effort to significantly improve.
While they wouldn’t accept mediocrity in any other area of their lives, many leaders celebrate average when it comes to leadership.
Gable supposedly responded with a question he asked everyone with lofty aspirations when they sought his advice: “How important is it to you?
If it’s not important to you, the likelihood that you will endure what it takes to become great is decidedly small.
Before embarking on an endeavor to improve as a leader, the first question to ask is: “How important is it to you?
Everyone else is waiting for your answer and the skills you have yet to improve.
